content:
Yesterday we saw the male goat as the sin offering; We have now completed our study of the sin offering; the one male goat, the singularity of atonement, the one sufficient sacrifice that covers the one root of sin. Now we move to the final and largest part of the dedication offering: the peace offerings. Numbers 7:17 lists them: two oxen, five rams, five male goats, and five male lambs of the first year. Seventeen animals in total, compared to one for the sin offering and three for the burnt offering. The peace offering was the most abundant offering of the entire dedication. More animals, more variety, more expression. And this abundance is itself a message. But before we look at what the animals say,
we need to understand what a peace offering was, why it was given, and what it meant in the life of Israel.

The Hebrew word for the peace offering is shelem, from the root shalom. Shalom does not simply mean the absence of conflict. It is one of the richest words in the Hebrew language. It means wholeness, completeness, health, wellbeing, harmony, and restored relationship. Shalom is the state of everything being in its right place, every broken thing made whole, every severed connection restored. To have shalom is not simply to be free from trouble; it is to be fully at rest in a life that is rightly ordered before God and rightly connected to others.

The peace offering was the only offering in Israel’s entire sacrificial system where three parties ate together from the same animal. The fat was burned on the altar as God’s portion. The breast was given to the priests as their portion. And the rest of the meat was returned to the offerer and his household to eat before Yahweh. God, the priest, and the worshipper at the same table, sharing the same sacrifice. No other offering did this. The burnt offering was entirely consumed God’s alone. The sin offering was for atonement the priest ate a portion but it was not a celebration. But the peace offering was a feast. It was three parties sitting down together because the separation between them had been dealt with and fellowship had been restored.

The peace offering was brought in different circumstances. It was brought as a thanksgiving offering when someone experienced a great blessing or deliverance from Yahweh (Leviticus 7:12). It was brought as a vow offering when a person had made a promise to God and was now fulfilling it (Leviticus 7:16). And it was brought as a freewill offering; simply because the worshipper wanted to express love and devotion to God without any specific occasion demanding it (Leviticus 7:16). Thanksgiving, vow, and freewill. Three reasons for the same offering. And all three came from the same place: a heart that had experienced the reality of restored relationship with Yahweh and wanted to celebrate it openly.

The order in which the offerings were brought to the altar is deeply significant. In Numbers 7, the burnt offering came first. Then the sin offering. Then the peace offering. This order was not merely ceremonial preference. It was theological necessity. The peace offering could only come after the burnt offering and the sin offering because peace with God can only come after the sin that broke the peace has been dealt with. You cannot have the feast before the atonement. You cannot sit down at the table before the debt at the door has been paid.

Romans 5:1 captures this order with perfect clarity: “Therefore, since we have been justified by faith, we have peace with God through our Lord Jesus Christ.” Therefore. The peace follows the justification. The shalom follows the atonement. We do not begin with peace and add atonement somewhere along the way. The burnt offering of total surrender and the sin offering of substitution came first. And then; only then can the peace offering be placed on the altar with joy. The seventeen animals of the peace offering could only come after the three of the burnt offering and the one of the sin offering had been laid down. The abundance of the peace rests entirely on the sufficiency of the atonement that preceded it.

Every aspect of the peace offering points to what Christ accomplished and who He is. Ephesians 2:14 says: “For He Himself is our peace, who has made us both one and has broken down in His flesh the dividing wall of hostility.”
He Himself is our peace. Not a feeling of peace. Not a temporary resolution of conflict. He is shalom in person; the wholeness, the completeness, the restored relationship embodied in a living being. The peace offering required an animal through which three parties could be brought to the same table. Christ is the one through whom God, the priesthood of believers, and the whole human family are brought to the same table.

Colossians 1:19-20 describes the full scope of what Christ’s peace offering accomplished: “For in Him all the fullness of God was pleased to dwell,
and through Christ to reconcile to Yahweh all things, whether on earth or in heaven, making peace by the blood of His cross.” Making peace by the blood of His cross. The peace offering required blood; the animal had to be killed.
The fat rose to God as the burnt portion. The priests received their share.
And the worshipper took the rest home to the family table. At the cross, the blood of Christ was shed. God received the offering. The priesthood of the new covenant received its portion of grace and calling. And the entire human family all things on earth was invited to the table of reconciliation. The peace offering of Numbers 7 was played out on the largest possible stage at Calvary.

Isaiah 53:5 gives us the language of the peace offering applied to Christ with exact precision: “He was pierced for our transgressions; He was crushed for our iniquities; upon Him was the chastisement that brought us peace, and with His wounds we are healed.” The chastisement that brought us peace. The shalom came through the suffering. The feast of restored relationship came through the blood. The table of God, priest, and worshipper eating together came through the cross where Christ was the sacrifice, the priest, and the one who provided the meal all at once. He is the peace offering in its fullest, most complete form.

title: Prayer
text:
Yahweh, how great are Your works; Your thoughts are very deep (Psalm 92:5).
Yahweh, You are the God of peace, and Your peace passes all understanding (Philippians 4:7). We thank You that before You gave us a peace offering, You gave us atonement; that You did not invite us to the feast before the debt at the door was paid. We thank You that the burnt offering came first, the sin offering came next, so that when we arrive at the peace offering it rests on ground that is solid and true. We thank You that Christ is our shalom; not a feeling, not a temporary resolution, but a whole and complete and unbroken restored relationship sealed in His blood. Help us to understand today what it means to have peace with youl not the peace of a quiet life, but the shalom of a life in right relationship with the one who made it. In Christ’s name, amen.
